\section{The root-count random variable}

\begin{definition}[Root count]
For a modulus $m\ge1$ and a target $a\in\Zm{m}$,
\[
  X_m(a) \;=\; \#\{\,x\in\Zm{m} : x^2=a\,\}
  \;=\; \#\{\,j \bmod m : m\mid j^2-a\,\}.
\]
\end{definition}

$X_m(N)/m$ is the exact density with which $m$ divides the sieve values
$v(j)=j^2-N$ as $j$ runs over a full residue window; the naive baseline uses the
constant $1/m$ in its place.

\begin{theorem}[Mean preservation]\label{thm:mean}
For every modulus $m\ge1$, $\;\sum_{a\in\Zm{m}} X_m(a)=m$. Equivalently, the average
over $N$ of the true per-$N$ divisibility rate $X_m(N)/m$ is exactly the naive rate
$1/m$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Count the fibres of the squaring map $x\mapsto x^2$ on $\Zm{m}$. The domain has $m$
elements, each lies in exactly one fibre, and $X_m(a)$ is the cardinality of the fibre
over $a$. Summing fibre cardinalities recovers the domain.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Non-degeneracy]\label{thm:nondeg}
For $m\ge3$ there exists $a\in\Zm{m}$ with $X_m(a)=0$, and there exists $a$ with
$X_m(a)\ge2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Squaring identifies $x$ with $-x$, and for $m\ge3$ some $x$ satisfies $x\ne-x$, so the
image of the squaring map is a proper subset of $\Zm{m}$; any target outside the image
has $X_m=0$. Since the total is $m$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:mean} and some value is $0$,
some value must be at least $2$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The prime case: an exact two-point mixture}

Let $p$ be an odd prime and $\chi_p$ the quadratic character on $\Zm{p}$.

\begin{theorem}[Character formula]\label{thm:char}
For every $a\in\Zm{p}$, $X_p(a)=\chi_p(a)+1$; that is, $X_p(a)=2$ for a nonzero
square, $0$ for a non-residue, and $1$ for $a=0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The fibre of $x\mapsto x^2$ over a nonzero square is $\{\pm x_0\}$, of size two since
$p$ is odd; over a non-residue it is empty; over $0$ it is $\{0\}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
$\sum_a X_p(a)=p$, since $\sum_a \chi_p(a)=0$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Exact over-dispersion]\label{thm:var}
For every odd prime $p$, $\;\sum_{a\in\Zm{p}}(X_p(a)-1)^2=p-1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:char} the summand is $\chi_p(a)^2$, equal to $1$ for $a\ne0$ and
$0$ for $a=0$; there are $p-1$ nonzero targets.
\end{proof}

For a mean-one count supported in $\{0,1,2\}$ the value $p-1$ out of a maximum of $p$
is the extreme of over-dispersion: all but one target sit at the endpoints.

\begin{theorem}[Exact functional identity]\label{thm:func}
For every $g:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}$ and every odd prime $p$,
\[
  \sum_{a\in\Zm{p}} g\big(X_p(a)\big) \;=\; g(1) \;+\; \frac{p-1}{2}\big(g(2)+g(0)\big).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Split off $a=0$, contributing $g(1)$. On the punctured set write
$g(X_p(a))=\tfrac{g(2)+g(0)}{2}+\chi_p(a)\tfrac{g(2)-g(0)}{2}$, correct at both values
of $\chi_p$; sum, using $\sum_{a\ne0}\chi_p(a)=0$ and $\#\{a\ne0\}=p-1$.
\end{proof}

\section{The convexity mechanism}

\begin{theorem}[Mixture excess, arbitrary modulus and convex functional]\label{thm:jensen}
For every modulus $m\ge1$ and every convex $G:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$,
\[
  m\,G(1) \;\le\; \sum_{a\in\Zm{m}} G\big(X_m(a)\big).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply Jensen's inequality to the uniform measure on $\Zm{m}$:
$G\big(\tfrac1m\sum_a X_m(a)\big)\le\tfrac1m\sum_a G(X_m(a))$. By
Theorem~\ref{thm:mean} the left argument is $1$; multiply by $m$.
\end{proof}

The left-hand side is exactly the naive baseline --- the functional evaluated as if
every $N$ had the mean rate --- so the truth always sits above the baseline.

\begin{theorem}[Strictness]\label{thm:strict}
For every $m\ge3$ and every strictly convex $G$,
$m\,G(1) < \sum_{a\in\Zm{m}} G(X_m(a))$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $L$ be a supporting line of $G$ at $1$, so $G\ge L$ with equality only at $1$.
Summing $L$ over $a$ reproduces $m\,G(1)$ exactly, since $L$ is affine and
$\sum_a X_m(a)=m$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:nondeg} some target has $X_m\ne1$, where
$G>L$ strictly; hence the summed inequality is strict.
\end{proof}

Primality is nowhere used: mean preservation plus non-constancy is the entire
mechanism, and quadratic reciprocity only fixes the size of the effect.

\subsection{The multiplicative proxy}

\begin{theorem}[Generating identity]\label{thm:gen}
For every odd prime $p$ and every real $c$,
\[
  \sum_{a\in\Zm{p}} c^{\,X_p(a)}
  \;=\; \underbrace{p\,c}_{\text{naive baseline}}
  \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{(p-1)(c-1)^2}{2}}_{\text{mixture excess}} .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:func} with $g(x)=c^x$ gives $c+\tfrac{p-1}{2}(c^2+1)$; rearrange with
$c^2+1=(c-1)^2+2c$.
\end{proof}

The excess is quadratic in $c-1$: a second-order variance effect, exactly as mean
preservation demands. There is no first-order shift.

\begin{definition}[Excess ratio]
For an odd prime $q$ and $c>0$, $\;E_q(c)=\dfrac{\sum_{a} c^{\,X_q(a)}}{q\,c}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Closed form and strictness]\label{thm:excess}
For an odd prime $q$ and $c>0$,
$E_q(c)=1+\big(1-\tfrac1q\big)X$ with $X=\dfrac{(c-1)^2}{2c}$, and $E_q(c)>1$
whenever $c\ne1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Divide Theorem~\ref{thm:gen} by $qc$ and simplify; $X>0$ for $c\ne1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Independence and product law]
For distinct odd primes $q_1,\dots,q_k$ and weights $c_1,\dots,c_k>0$, summing the
product proxy over the product of residue systems --- isomorphic to
$\Zm{(q_1\cdots q_k)}$ by the Chinese remainder theorem --- factorises:
\[
  \sum_{N}\ \prod_i c_i^{\,X_{q_i}(N_i)} \;=\; \prod_i \sum_{a} c_i^{\,X_{q_i}(a)} .
\]
If every $c_i\ne1$ then $\prod_i (q_i c_i) < \sum_N \prod_i c_i^{X_{q_i}(N_i)}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Expansion of a product of sums, then Theorem~\ref{thm:excess} factor by factor.
\end{proof}

\section{No single carrier}

\begin{definition}[Hump log-amplitude]
For a mixture over odd primes $q_1,\dots,q_k$ with common weight $c$,
\[
  A=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\ell_i,\qquad
  \ell_i=\log E_{q_i}(c)=\log\!\Big(1+\big(1-\tfrac{1}{q_i}\big)X\Big),\qquad
  X=\frac{(c-1)^2}{2c}.
\]
\end{definition}

The shape factor $X$ is common to all primes; the only prime-dependence is the bounded
factor $1-1/q\in[2/3,1)$.

\begin{lemma}[Concavity squeeze]\label{lem:squeeze}
For $Y\ge0$ and $\theta\in[0,1]$, $\;\theta\log(1+Y)\le\log(1+\theta Y)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Concavity of $\log$ applied to the points $1$ and $1+Y$ with weights $1-\theta$ and
$\theta$, using $\log1=0$ and $(1-\theta)\cdot1+\theta(1+Y)=1+\theta Y$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Two-sided per-prime squeeze]\label{thm:pps}
For every odd prime $q$ and $c>0$, with $L=\log(1+X)$, one has
$\tfrac23 L\le \ell_q\le L$. More finely, with $Y_q=(1-1/q)X$,
\[
  \frac{Y_q}{1+Y_q}\;\le\;\ell_q\;\le\;Y_q .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Upper bound: $1-1/q<1$ and $\log$ is increasing (and $\log(1+y)\le y$). Lower bound:
$1-1/q\ge2/3$ for $q\ge3$, so $\ell_q\ge\log(1+\tfrac23X)\ge\tfrac23\log(1+X)$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:squeeze}; and $\log(1+y)\ge y/(1+y)$ for $y\ge0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[No single carrier]\label{thm:nocarrier}
In a mixture over $k$ odd primes, each prime's share obeys
$\ell_j/A \le 3/(2k)$. Hence if $k\ge3$ no single prime accounts for more than $50\%$
of the amplitude --- strictly below the registered $60\%$ removal bar --- and if
$k\ge5$ no single prime accounts for more than $30\%$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:pps}, $A\ge k\cdot\tfrac23 L$ and $\ell_j\le L$, so
$\ell_j\le L\le \tfrac{3}{2k}A$. Substituting $k=3,5$ gives $1/2$ and $3/10$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Residual hump]\label{cor:residual}
Let $R_j=A-\ell_j$ be the amplitude surviving removal of the single covariate
$q_j\mid v$. For $k\ge3$, $R_j\ge\tfrac12 A>0$.
\end{corollary}

This is the formal content of the experimental $0\%$-removal table: the result is
structural, not statistical. No amount of data can make a single per-hit binary
covariate carry more than $3/(2k)$ of a divisibility-mixture hump.

\begin{theorem}[Carrier-count bracket]\label{thm:tomography}
For a $k$-prime mixture with weight $c\ne1$ and $X=(c-1)^2/(2c)$,
\[
  \frac{A}{X}\;\le\;k\;\le\;\frac{3}{2}\cdot\frac{A}{\log(1+X)} .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\ell_i\le\log(1+X)\le X$ gives $A\le kX$, hence the left inequality;
$\ell_i\ge\tfrac23\log(1+X)$ gives $A\ge\tfrac{2k}{3}\log(1+X)$, hence the right.
\end{proof}

The bracket is tight up to the factor $\tfrac32 X/\log(1+X)$, which tends to $\tfrac32$
as $X\to0$.

\section{From amplitude to spread: the Dickman dictionary}

The mixture picture says the effective Dickman argument $u=\log v/\log B$ is not a
single number per hit but a small distribution: values inheriting extra small prime
factors behave as though their argument were slightly reduced. Fitting an exact
Dickman baseline --- evaluating $\rho$ at the mean argument --- necessarily
under-predicts, by Proposition~\ref{prop:convex}.

\begin{definition}[Two-point hump amplitude]
For $u>0$ and $\delta$ with $u-\delta>0$,
\[
  H(u,\delta)=\frac{\rho_1(u)+\rho_1(u-\delta)}{2}-\rho_1\!\Big(u-\frac{\delta}{2}\Big).
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Closed form]\label{thm:hump}
For $u>0$ and $0<u-\delta$,
\[
  H(u,\delta)\;=\;\frac12\log\!\left(1+\frac{\delta^2}{4\,u\,(u-\delta)}\right).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
With $\rho_1(x)=1-\log x$ the constants cancel and
$H=\log(u-\tfrac\delta2)-\tfrac12\log u-\tfrac12\log(u-\delta)
=\tfrac12\log\frac{(u-\delta/2)^2}{u(u-\delta)}$; the identity
$(u-\delta/2)^2=u(u-\delta)+\delta^2/4$ finishes.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Faithfulness and positivity]
$H(u,0)=0$, and $H(u,\delta)>0$ whenever $\delta\ne0$ and $u-\delta>0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The logarithm's argument in Theorem~\ref{thm:hump} equals $1$ at $\delta=0$ and
exceeds $1$ otherwise.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Strict monotonicity in the spread]\label{thm:mono}
For fixed $u>0$, $\delta\mapsto H(u,\delta)$ is strictly increasing on $[0,u)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
It suffices that $\delta\mapsto\delta^2/(4u(u-\delta))$ is strictly increasing. For
$0\le a<b<u$, cross-multiplication gives
$b^2\,4u(u-a)-a^2\,4u(u-b)=4u(b-a)\big(u(a+b)-ab\big)$, and $u(a+b)-ab>0$ since
$u>a\ge0$ and $b>0$ give $ub>ab$ while $ua\ge0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Calibrated spread]
For $u>0$ and $A>0$ put $s=e^{2A}-1$ and
$\;\delta(u,A)=2u\big(\sqrt{s^2+s}-s\big)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Admissibility]\label{thm:adm}
For every $u>0$ and $A>0$, $\;0<\delta(u,A)<u$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$A>0$ gives $s>0$; then $s^2+s>s^2$ yields $\sqrt{s^2+s}>s$, so $\delta>0$. Also
$(s+\tfrac12)^2=s^2+s+\tfrac14>s^2+s$, so $\sqrt{s^2+s}<s+\tfrac12$ and
$\delta<2u\cdot\tfrac12=u$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact calibration]\label{thm:cal}
For every $u>0$ and $A>0$, $\;H\big(u,\delta(u,A)\big)=A$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $t=\sqrt{s^2+s}-s$, so $\delta=2ut$ and $t^2+2st-s=0$, i.e. $t^2=s(1-2t)$; by
Theorem~\ref{thm:adm}, $1-2t>0$. Then
\[
  \frac{\delta^2}{4u(u-\delta)}=\frac{4u^2t^2}{4u\cdot u(1-2t)}
  =\frac{t^2}{1-2t}=s=e^{2A}-1,
\]
so the argument of the logarithm in Theorem~\ref{thm:hump} is $e^{2A}$ and
$H=\tfrac12\cdot2A=A$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Scale freedom]\label{thm:scale}
$\delta(u,A)=u\cdot\delta(1,A)$: the relative spread $\delta/u$ depends only on the
measured amplitude.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$u$ appears in the definition only as an overall factor.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Synthesis}

\begin{theorem}[Mixture--hump identification]
Let $A=\sum_i\log E_{q_i}(c)>0$ be the log-amplitude generated by a nonempty
quadratic-residue divisibility mixture over odd primes with weight $c\ne1$, and let
$u>0$. Then $\delta(u,A)\in(0,u)$ and $H(u,\delta(u,A))=A$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$A>0$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:excess}; apply Theorems~\ref{thm:adm} and~\ref{thm:cal}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Monotone comparability]
For $u>0$ and $0<A<B$, $\;\delta(u,A)<\delta(u,B)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Both lie in $[0,u)$; if $\delta(u,A)\ge\delta(u,B)$ then Theorem~\ref{thm:mono}
(or equality) with Theorem~\ref{thm:cal} would give $A\ge B$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The residual is still a hump]
With $k\ge3$ primes, for any $j$ the residual amplitude $R_j=A-\ell_j$ satisfies
$R_j\ge\tfrac12A>0$, its calibrated spread $\delta(u,R_j)$ is admissible,
$H(u,\delta(u,R_j))=R_j$, and $\delta(u,\tfrac12A)\le\delta(u,R_j)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Combine Corollary~\ref{cor:residual} with Theorems~\ref{thm:adm}, \ref{thm:cal} and
monotone comparability.
\end{proof}

\section{Numerical illustration}

Take $c=3/2$, so $X=(c-1)^2/(2c)=1/12\approx0.08333$.

\begin{itemize}
\item For $p=7$: $\sum_a c^{X_7(a)}=7c+3(c-1)^2=10.5+0.75=11.25$, matching
brute-force enumeration of the root counts $(1,2,2,0,2,0,0)$, namely
$c+3c^2+3=11.25$. Thus $E_7(3/2)=15/14\approx1.0714$ and $\log E_7\approx0.06899$.
\item For $p=13$: $\sum_a c^{X_{13}(a)}=13c+6(c-1)^2=19.5+1.5=21$ exactly.
\item Over-dispersion: $\sum_a (X_{11}(a)-1)^2=10=11-1$.
\end{itemize}

Over the odd primes $3,5,7,11,13$ at $c=3/2$,
\[
  A\approx0.0541+0.0645+0.0690+0.0730+0.0741\approx0.3347,
\]
with per-prime shares from $16.2\%$ to $22.1\%$ --- inside the guaranteed ceiling
$3/(2\cdot5)=30\%$ and far below the $60\%$ bar. The tomography bracket reads
$A/X\approx4.02\le k=5\le\tfrac32A/\log(1+X)\approx6.27$.

Calibrating the measured amplitude $A=0.1163$ at $u=2$: $s=e^{0.2326}-1\approx0.26187$,
$\sqrt{s^2+s}\approx0.57485$, hence $\delta\approx1.2519$ and $\delta/u\approx0.626$;
substituting back reproduces $H(2,1.2519)=0.1163$ to machine precision, and the
relative spread is the same at every $u$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:scale}.

\section{Algorithms}

\paragraph{Exact mixture baseline.} Rather than predicting sieve yield by
$\rho(\log v/\log B)$, compute for the actual modulus $N$ the true small-prime
densities $X_q(N)/q$ for all $q\le Q$ and use the resulting mixture as the baseline.
Cost: one Legendre-symbol evaluation per small prime, $O(\pi(Q)\log N)$ overall.

\paragraph{Amplitude calibration.} Given a fitted amplitude $A$ and reference argument
$u$, return $\delta(u,A)$; constant time, exact by Theorem~\ref{thm:cal}, scale-free by
Theorem~\ref{thm:scale}.

\paragraph{Carrier-count tomography.} Given $A$ and $c$, return the bracket of
Theorem~\ref{thm:tomography}; constant time, and the interval provably contains the
number of participating primes under the mixture model.

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{What was mis-specified}

The naive baseline is not wrong about average behaviour --- Theorem~\ref{thm:mean}
shows it is exactly right there. It is wrong about conditional behaviour: for a fixed
$N$ every small prime has already made a binary decision (residue vs. non-residue)
fixing its divisibility density at $2/q$ or $0$, never $1/q$. Averaging over $N$ hides
this; sieving a single $N$ exposes it. Since the smoothness functional is convex in
the densities, the concealed structure always pushes the yield up, so the direction of
the observed hump is compelled by the arithmetic.

\subsection{Why the negative result is the strong one}

A common failure mode in large computational experiments is to keep testing binary
features until one appears to explain an anomaly. Theorem~\ref{thm:nocarrier}
forecloses that search analytically: no per-hit binary covariate can remove more than
$3/(2k)$ of a $k$-prime mixture hump, so with even a handful of small primes a $60\%$
bar is unreachable by construction. The uniform $0\%$ removal table is therefore a
confirmation of the mechanism, and the correct next model is a mixture over $v\bmod q$
for small $q$ rather than a covariate-augmented pointwise baseline. That divisibility
conditioning absorbed $45$--$60\%$ of the yes-stratum point amplitude while parity and
factor counts absorbed none fits precisely: conditioning on $q\mid v$ partially freezes
one factor of the product law, removing that factor's bounded share.

\subsection{Scope and caveats}

The identification is a model identification: it assumes the effective Dickman
argument is well approximated by a two-point mixture and prices the hump on the first
Dickman branch, where $\rho(u)=1-\log u$. Extending past $u=2$ needs the higher
branches, which are not elementary; positivity and monotonicity persist by convexity,
but the exact inversion is branch-specific. The shared-factor covariate could not be
tested in the reported experiment because at $96$ bits the prime factors of $N$ vastly
exceed the sieve window, making that stratum structurally empty rather than merely
quiet; and a factor-count statistic capped at $100$ ignores prime factors above $100$
by definition.

\subsection{Robustness}

Only two properties of $j^2-N$ were used: the root count has mean $1$ over targets and
is not constant. Replacing $j^2$ by an arbitrary sieve polynomial $f(j)$ leaves the
fibre-counting proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:mean} untouched, so the convexity excess of
Theorems~\ref{thm:jensen} and~\ref{thm:strict} persists verbatim; only the size of the
excess, controlled by the splitting behaviour of $f$ modulo $q$, changes. Prime-power
and composite moduli are likewise already covered; only the exact quantitative
identities use the residue dichotomy.

\section{Future work}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Prime-power and composite carriers.} Mean preservation holds at every
modulus, so only the shape of the root-count distribution distinguishes moduli; for
$m=p^k$ that shape is governed by Hensel lifting and stratification by the $p$-adic
valuation of the target. The general inequality is settled; the exact size of the
effect remains, a finite computation.
\item \textbf{Higher-degree sieve polynomials.} For $f(j)-N$ the mean-preservation
argument transfers verbatim, and the shape of the excess should be governed by the
splitting behaviour of $f$ modulo $q$ --- a Galois-theoretic invariant rather than
quadratic reciprocity. The variance identity and the stratum sizes need the degree-$d$
analogue.
\item \textbf{Weighted mixtures.} Realistic proxies weight $q$ by $\log q/\log B$; the
per-prime squeeze and the $3/(2k)$ ceiling then need weighted analogues.
\item \textbf{Beyond the first Dickman branch.} Extend the closed-form hump and its
inversion to $u>2$, where $\rho$ has no elementary expression.
\item \textbf{Sharpening the tomography.} The bracket loses a factor near $3/2$ from
the worst case $q=3$; using the actual primes present should shrink it to
near-determinacy.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Conclusion}

A three-sigma hump over an exact Dickman baseline in the smoothness rate of $j^2-N$
has an exact arithmetic explanation and admits no single-covariate carrier, and both
facts are theorems rather than observations. Mean preservation holds at every modulus;
the per-$N$ rate is nevertheless a genuine two-point mixture with maximal
over-dispersion $\sum_N(X_p(N)-1)^2=p-1$; convexity forces a strictly positive excess,
quadratic in $c-1$; each prime's share of the log-amplitude is capped at $3/(2k)$,
defeating a $60\%$ removal bar already at $k\ge3$; and the amplitude itself, through
$\tfrac12\log(1+\delta^2/(4u(u-\delta)))$ and its exact scale-free inversion, measures
the spread of the underlying mixture. The practical upshot is a replacement baseline
for sieve yield prediction: a divisibility mixture over residue classes of $N$ modulo
the small primes.

from __future__ import annotations

import math
import random
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Root counts and mean preservation
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def root_counts(m: int) -> List[int]:
    """X_m(a) = #{x mod m : x^2 = a} for every target a in Z/m."""
    counts = [0] * m
    for x in range(m):
        counts[(x * x) % m] += 1
    return counts


def mean_preservation_check(m: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Return (sum of root counts, m).  The theorem says they are equal."""
    return sum(root_counts(m)), m


def over_dispersion(p: int) -> int:
    """sum_a (X_p(a) - 1)^2 ; equals p - 1 for every odd prime p."""
    return sum((c - 1) ** 2 for c in root_counts(p))


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Exact functional / generating identities
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def functional_sum_bruteforce(p: int, g: Callable[[int], float]) -> float:
    """sum_a g(X_p(a)) by direct enumeration."""
    return sum(g(c) for c in root_counts(p))


def functional_sum_formula(p: int, g: Callable[[int], float]) -> float:
    """g(1) + (p-1)(g(2)+g(0))/2 -- the exact functional identity."""
    return g(1) + (p - 1) * (g(2) + g(0)) / 2.0


def generating_sum_formula(p: int, c: float) -> float:
    """p c + (p-1)(c-1)^2/2 -- naive baseline plus mixture excess."""
    return p * c + (p - 1) * (c - 1) ** 2 / 2.0


def excess_ratio(q: int, c: float) -> float:
    """E_q(c) = 1 + (1 - 1/q) (c-1)^2 / (2c)."""
    return 1.0 + (1.0 - 1.0 / q) * shape_factor(c)


def shape_factor(c: float) -> float:
    """X = (c-1)^2 / (2c), the prime-independent shape of the excess."""
    return (c - 1.0) ** 2 / (2.0 * c)


def log_excess(q: int, c: float) -> float:
    """Per-prime contribution to the hump log-amplitude."""
    return math.log(excess_ratio(q, c))


def hump_log_amplitude(primes: Sequence[int], c: float) -> float:
    """A = sum_q log E_q(c)."""
    return sum(log_excess(q, c) for q in primes)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Convexity mechanism
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def jensen_gap(m: int, G: Callable[[float], float]) -> float:
    """sum_a G(X_m(a)) - m G(1) ; nonnegative for convex G, positive for m>=3
    and strictly convex G."""
    return sum(G(float(c)) for c in root_counts(m)) - m * G(1.0)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Dickman branch, hump, calibration
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def rho1(u: float) -> float:
    """First Dickman branch rho(u) = 1 - log u, valid on [1, 2]."""
    return 1.0 - math.log(u)


def hump_amp_definition(u: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """(rho(u) + rho(u-d))/2 - rho(u - d/2), computed from the definition."""
    return (rho1(u) + rho1(u - delta)) / 2.0 - rho1(u - delta / 2.0)


def hump_amp_closed_form(u: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """(1/2) log(1 + d^2 / (4 u (u - d)))."""
    return 0.5 * math.log(1.0 + delta ** 2 / (4.0 * u * (u - delta)))


def calibrated_spread(u: float, A: float) -> float:
    """Exact inverse: the spread reproducing a measured amplitude A."""
    s = math.exp(2.0 * A) - 1.0
    return 2.0 * u * (math.sqrt(s * s + s) - s)


def carrier_count_bracket(A: float, c: float) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """A/X <= k <= (3/2) A / log(1+X) with X = (c-1)^2/(2c)."""
    X = shape_factor(c)
    return A / X, 1.5 * A / math.log(1.0 + X)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. A direct sieve experiment
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def sieve_divisibility_rate(N: int, q: int, window: int) -> float:
    """Observed density of q | (j^2 - N) for j in a window above sqrt(N)."""
    j0 = math.isqrt(N) + 1
    hits = sum(1 for j in range(j0, j0 + window) if (j * j - N) % q == 0)
    return hits / window


def legendre_root_count(N: int, q: int) -> int:
    """Predicted X_q(N) = number of solutions of j^2 = N mod q."""
    return sum(1 for x in range(q) if (x * x - N) % q == 0)

def demo_dickman_hump() -> None:
    section("6.  The Dickman two-point hump and its exact calibration")
    print("Closed form  H(u,d) = (1/2) log(1 + d^2/(4u(u-d)))  vs. the definition:")
    print(f"{'u':>6} {'delta':>8} {'definition':>14} {'closed form':>14} {'diff':>10}")

        for frac in [0.0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8]:
            d = frac * u
            a1 = hump_amp_definition(u, d)
            a2 = hump_amp_closed_form(u, d)
            print(f"{u:>6.2f} {d:>8.4f} {a1:>14.10f} {a2:>14.10f} {abs(a1-a2):>10.2e}")

    print("\nStrict monotonicity in the spread (u = 2):")
    prev = -1.0
    for frac in [0.0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 0.95]:
        val = hump_amp_closed_form(2.0, frac * 2.0) if frac > 0 else 0.0

        print(f"   delta/u = {frac:>5.2f}   H = {val:.8f}"
              f"   {'increasing' if val > prev else ''}")
        prev = val

    print("\nExact inversion  d(u,A) = 2u(sqrt(s^2+s) - s),  s = exp(2A)-1:")
    print(f"{'u':>6} {'A':>10} {'delta':>12} {'delta/u':>10} {'H(u,delta)':>14} {'diff':>10}")
    for u in [1.5, 2.0, 4.0, 10.0]:
        for A in [0.02, 0.1163, 0.3, 1.0]:
            d = calibrated_spread(u, A)
            back = hump_amp_closed_form(u, d)
            print(f"{u:>6.2f} {A:>10.4f} {d:>12.6f} {d/u:>10.6f} {back:>14.10f}"
                  f" {abs(back - A):>10.2e}")
    print("\nNote the delta/u column: identical down the rows for fixed A.")
    print("The calibration is scale free.")

    A_measured, A_err = 0.1163, 0.0360
    print(f"\nMeasured amplitude A = {A_measured} +/- {A_err} (z = 3.23):")
    for u in [1.5, 2.0, 2.5]:
        d = calibrated_spread(u, A_measured)
        dlo = calibrated_spread(u, max(A_measured - A_err, 1e-9))
        dhi = calibrated_spread(u, A_measured + A_err)
        print(f"   u = {u:.2f}:  delta = {d:.5f}  (1-sigma band "

    print("Control amplitude 0.0269 +/- 0.0109 gives, for comparison, "
          f"delta/u = {calibrated_spread(1.0, 0.0269):.5f}.")


def demo_sieve_experiment(seed: int = 20260826) -> None:
    section("7.  A direct sieve experiment on v = j^2 - N")
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    window = 20000
    print(f"window of {window} consecutive j above sqrt(N); "
          "naive baseline predicts density 1/q for every N")
    for q in [3, 5, 7, 11]:
        print(f"\n  small prime q = {q}   (naive 1/q = {1/q:.5f}, "
              f"true rate is X_q(N)/q in {{0, {2/q:.5f}}} or {1/q:.5f} if q | N)")
        rates: List[float] = []
        for _ in range(8):
            N = rng.randrange(10 ** 14, 10 ** 15) | 1
            observed = sieve_divisibility_rate(N, q, window)
            predicted = legendre_root_count(N, q) / q
            rates.append(observed)
            print(f"    N mod {q} = {N % q}:  X_q(N) = {legendre_root_count(N, q)}"
                  f"   predicted {predicted:.5f}   observed {observed:.5f}")
        print(f"    mean of observed rates over these N: {sum(rates)/len(rates):.5f}"
              f"  (population mean is exactly {1/q:.5f})")
    print("\nEvery individual N is off the naive rate; the AVERAGE is exactly on it.")
    print("That is mean preservation, and convexity turns it into a positive hump.")

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple


def sieve_of_eratosthenes(limit: int) -> List[int]:
    """All primes <= limit."""
    flags = bytearray([1]) * (limit + 1)
    flags[0:2] = b"\x00\x00"
    for p in range(2, int(limit ** 0.5) + 1):
        if flags[p]:
            flags[p * p:: p] = bytearray(len(flags[p * p:: p]))
    return [i for i, f in enumerate(flags) if f]


def legendre_symbol(a: int, p: int) -> int:
    """Legendre symbol (a|p) for an odd prime p, by Euler's criterion."""
    a %= p
    if a == 0:
        return 0
    t = pow(a, (p - 1) // 2, p)
    return 1 if t == 1 else -1


def root_count_mod_prime(N: int, q: int) -> int:
    """X_q(N) = number of solutions of j^2 = N (mod q), for odd prime q."""
    return legendre_symbol(N, q) + 1


def exact_divisibility_densities(N: int, bound: int) -> Dict[int, float]:
    """True density X_q(N)/q of q | (j^2 - N), for every odd prime q <= bound.

    The naive baseline would return 1/q for all of them.
    """
    return {q: root_count_mod_prime(N, q) / q
            for q in sieve_of_eratosthenes(bound) if q != 2}


def naive_densities(bound: int) -> Dict[int, float]:
    """The mis-specified baseline: density 1/q for every odd prime q <= bound."""
    return {q: 1.0 / q for q in sieve_of_eratosthenes(bound) if q != 2}


def mixture_log_excess(N: int, bound: int, c: float) -> float:
    """Log-excess of the exact mixture over the naive baseline for the
    multiplicative smoothness proxy with weight c per divisibility hit.

    Population form (averaged over N): sum_q log(1 + (1 - 1/q)(c-1)^2/(2c)).
    Per-N form (used here): sum_q [ X_q(N) log c - log(naive expectation) ].
    """
    X = (c - 1.0) ** 2 / (2.0 * c)
    return sum(math.log(1.0 + (1.0 - 1.0 / q) * X)
               for q in sieve_of_eratosthenes(bound) if q != 2)


def mean_preservation_audit(bound: int, sample: int = 2048,
                            seed: int = 20260826) -> List[Tuple[int, float, float]]:
    """Empirical check that averaging the exact densities over N recovers 1/q.

    Returns a list of (q, average exact density, naive density 1/q).
    """
    import random
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    primes = [q for q in sieve_of_eratosthenes(bound) if q != 2]
    Ns = [rng.randrange(10 ** 12, 10 ** 13) | 1 for _ in range(sample)]
    out: List[Tuple[int, float, float]] = []
    for q in primes:
        avg = sum(root_count_mod_prime(N, q) / q for N in Ns) / len(Ns)
        out.append((q, avg, 1.0 / q))
    return out

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import List, NamedTuple, Sequence, Tuple


class Calibration(NamedTuple):
    amplitude: float
    argument: float
    spread: float
    relative_spread: float
    round_trip: float
    admissible: bool


def hump_amplitude(u: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """H(u, delta) = (1/2) log(1 + delta^2 / (4 u (u - delta)))."""
    if delta == 0.0:
        return 0.0
    if not (0.0 < u and delta < u):
        raise ValueError("require 0 < delta < u")
    return 0.5 * math.log(1.0 + delta ** 2 / (4.0 * u * (u - delta)))


def calibrate(u: float, A: float) -> Calibration:
    """Invert the hump exactly: delta = 2u( sqrt(s^2+s) - s ), s = exp(2A) - 1."""
    if u <= 0.0 or A <= 0.0:
        raise ValueError("require u > 0 and A > 0")
    s = math.exp(2.0 * A) - 1.0
    delta = 2.0 * u * (math.sqrt(s * s + s) - s)
    return Calibration(
        amplitude=A,
        argument=u,
        spread=delta,
        relative_spread=delta / u,     # independent of u: scale free
        round_trip=hump_amplitude(u, delta),
        admissible=(0.0 < delta < u),
    )


def shape_factor(c: float) -> float:
    """X = (c - 1)^2 / (2c)."""
    return (c - 1.0) ** 2 / (2.0 * c)


def carrier_bracket(A: float, c: float) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """A/X <= k <= (3/2) A / log(1 + X): the number of participating primes."""
    if c <= 0.0 or c == 1.0:
        raise ValueError("require c > 0, c != 1")
    X = shape_factor(c)
    return A / X, 1.5 * A / math.log(1.0 + X)


def max_single_share(k: int) -> float:
    """The guaranteed ceiling 3/(2k) on any single prime's share."""
    if k < 1:
        raise ValueError("require k >= 1")
    return 3.0 / (2.0 * k)


def carrier_is_possible(k: int, bar: float = 0.60) -> bool:
    """Can a single per-hit binary covariate clear the removal bar?"""
    return max_single_share(k) > bar

    ls = [math.log(1.0 + (1.0 - 1.0 / q) * X) for q in primes]
    A = sum(ls)
    return [l / A for l in ls]

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import List

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def shape_factor(c: float) -> float:
    """X = (c-1)^2 / (2c) — common to every prime."""
    return (c - 1.0) ** 2 / (2.0 * c)


def log_excess(q: int, c: float) -> float:
    """Per-prime hump contribution log E_q(c) = log(1 + (1-1/q) X)."""
    return math.log(1.0 + (1.0 - 1.0 / q) * shape_factor(c))


def root_counts(m: int) -> List[int]:
    """X_m(a) = #{x mod m : x^2 = a}."""
    counts = [0] * m
    for x in range(m):
        counts[(x * x) % m] += 1
    return counts


def main() -> None:
    primes = [3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19]
    c = 1.4
    k = len(primes)
    shares = [log_excess(q, c) for q in primes]
    A = sum(shares)
    shares = [s / A for s in shares]

    ax2.set_ylabel("root count")
    var = sum((x - 1) ** 2 for x in counts)
    ax2.set_title(rf"Exact two-point mixture: mean $={sum(counts)/p:.0f}$, "
                  rf"$\sum_a (X_p(a)-1)^2={var}=p-1$")
    ax2.set_xticks(range(p))
    ax2.legend(fontsize=9)
    ax2.grid(alpha=0.25, axis="y")

  "interactive_layout": "# Why a Factoring Sieve Beats Its Own Textbook Prediction

*A guided tour of the divisibility-mixture baseline: how a three-sigma bump in a
smoothness rate turns out to be Jensen's inequality wearing a disguise, why no
single divisibility flag can be blamed for it, and how to read the bump as a
measurement.*

---

## 1. The setting in one paragraph

To factor a large number $N$, one of the oldest good ideas is to walk $j$ upward from
$\lceil\sqrt N\rceil$ and inspect the values

$$v = j^2 - N.$$

If enough of these values are *smooth* — factoring completely into primes below a
bound $B$ — then linear algebra over $\mathbb{F}_2$ delivers a factorization of $N$.
Everything about the cost of such an algorithm reduces to one question: **how often is
$v$ smooth?**

The textbook answer is the Dickman function $\rho$, defined as the unique continuous
solution of the delay differential equation

$$u\,\rho'(u) = -\rho(u-1), \qquad \rho \equiv 1 \text{ on } [0,1],$$

evaluated at $u = \log v/\log B$. On the first interesting stretch $1 \le u \le 2$ it
has the elementary closed form $\rho(u) = 1 - \log u$.

<details>
<summary><b>Background: what is a smooth number, and why does the Dickman function appear?</b></summary>

An integer is *$B$-smooth* if all of its prime factors are at most $B$. The Dickman
function answers the question "what fraction of integers up to $x$ are
$x^{1/u}$-smooth?" — the answer tends to $\rho(u)$ as $x \to \infty$. Intuitively,
$\rho$ is built by a recursive argument on the *largest* prime factor: conditioning on
it produces exactly the delay equation above. On $[1,2]$ one integrates directly:
$\rho'(u) = -1/u$ with $\rho(1)=1$ gives $\rho(u) = 1 - \log u$. Past $u = 2$ the
solution stops being elementary and decays roughly like $u^{-u}$, which is why sieve
parameters are chosen so carefully. Further reading:
[smooth numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_number),
[the Dickman function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dickman_function),
[the quadratic sieve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_sieve).
</details>

Fit that curve to real sieve data and the residual should be noise. In a large
experiment — 9,594 smooth hits, 512,000 controls, 128 moduli of 96 bits — it was not.
A hump of log-amplitude $A = 0.1163 \pm 0.0360$ (about $3.2$ standard deviations) sat
over the range $t \in [0.45, 0.85]$, while a matched random-integer control returned
$0.0269 \pm 0.0109$: nothing. The hump belongs to the arithmetic of $j^2 - N$.

---

## 2. The lie in the baseline

The naive baseline says a small prime $p$ divides a random integer with probability
$1/p$. But $v = j^2 - N$ is not random. For an odd prime $p$,

$$p \mid j^2 - N \iff j^2 \equiv N \pmod p,$$

and that congruence has $2$, $0$, or $1$ solutions according as $N$ is a nonzero
square mod $p$, a non-residue, or divisible by $p$. Write $X_p(N)$ for that count.
Then the true divisibility density is $X_p(N)/p$ — which is $2/p$ or $0$, **never**
$1/p$, for any individual $N$.

And yet the naive rate is not wrong *on average*:

$$\sum_{N \bmod m} \#\{\,j \bmod m : m \mid j^2 - N\,\} = m \qquad \text{for every modulus } m.$$

<details>
<summary><b>Proof of mean preservation (one line, no primality needed)</b></summary>

Count the fibres of the squaring map $x \mapsto x^2$ on $\mathbb{Z}/m$. Each of the $m$
elements of the domain lies in exactly one fibre, and $X_m(a)$ is the size of the fibre
over $a$; summing fibre sizes recovers the domain, which has $m$ elements. Nothing
about $m$ was used — this is pure counting, and it works for prime powers, composites,
and (with the same argument) for any sieve polynomial in place of $j^2$.
</details>

Let's watch this happen on real numbers. The routine below computes, for a concrete
modulus $N$, the true small-prime densities and compares them against the naive ones —
then averages over many $N$ to see the naive rate reappear exactly.

{{algorithm:0}}

---

## 3. Convexity turns the hidden structure into a hump

We now have a random variable with **mean exactly one** that is **never constant**.
That is all Jensen's inequality needs.

Smoothness is multiplicative: extra small prime divisors help, so the natural proxies
are convex functionals $G$ of the divisibility counts. For every convex $G$ and every
modulus $m$,

$$m\,G(1) \;\le\; \sum_{a \bmod m} G\big(X_m(a)\big),$$

with the left-hand side being *precisely* the naive baseline — the functional evaluated
as though every $N$ had the mean rate. For $m \ge 3$ and strictly convex $G$, the
inequality is strict. **The truth always beats the baseline, and it beats it upward.**

For odd primes we can do better than an inequality and compute the excess exactly:

$$\sum_{N \bmod p} c^{\,X_p(N)} \;=\; \underbrace{p\,c}_{\text{naive}} \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{(p-1)(c-1)^2}{2}}_{\text{excess}}.$$

<details>
<summary><b>Where that identity comes from — and why the shape matters</b></summary>

Every functional of the root count collapses onto three values, because the root count
only ever takes three values. Splitting off $a = 0$ (one target, one double root) and
writing the rest as an affine function of the Legendre symbol gives

$$\sum_{N \bmod p} g\big(X_p(N)\big) = g(1) + \frac{p-1}{2}\big(g(2) + g(0)\big),$$

since half of the nonzero targets are residues and half are not. Taking $g(x) = c^x$
and simplifying with $c^2 + 1 = (c-1)^2 + 2c$ yields the displayed identity.

The *shape* is the point. The excess is **quadratic in $c - 1$**: it is a variance
effect, not a shift of the mean — exactly what mean preservation demands. A companion
identity says the same thing directly: $\sum_N (X_p(N)-1)^2 = p - 1$, the maximum
possible over-dispersion for a mean-one count living in $\{0,1,2\}$.
</details>

Here is the picture. The chord is the mixture; the curve is the baseline; the gap is
the hump.

{{visualization:0}}

---

## 4. Play with it: the hump calibrator

Convexity says the gap is positive. The closed form says exactly how big it is. For a
symmetric two-point mixture of the Dickman argument with spread $\delta$,

$$H(u,\delta) \;=\; \frac{\rho(u) + \rho(u-\delta)}{2} - \rho\!\Big(u - \frac{\delta}{2}\Big) \;=\; \frac12\log\!\left(1 + \frac{\delta^2}{4u(u-\delta)}\right).$$

Drag the sliders below. Watch three things: the hump vanishes identically at zero
spread; it increases strictly and monotonically with the spread; and the inversion
panel takes any measured amplitude back to the spread that produced it — exactly, and
with the relative spread $\delta/u$ unchanged as you move $u$.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

<details>
<summary><b>The exact inversion, and why it always lands in the admissible range</b></summary>

Set $s = e^{2A} - 1$ and $\delta(u,A) = 2u(\sqrt{s^2+s} - s)$. Writing
$t = \sqrt{s^2+s} - s$, one checks $t^2 + 2st - s = 0$, i.e. $t^2 = s(1-2t)$. Then

$$\frac{\delta^2}{4u(u-\delta)} = \frac{4u^2t^2}{4u^2(1-2t)} = \frac{t^2}{1-2t} = s = e^{2A}-1,$$

so $H(u,\delta(u,A)) = \tfrac12\log e^{2A} = A$ exactly. Admissibility is two
inequalities: $\sqrt{s^2+s} > s$ gives $\delta > 0$, and
$(s+\tfrac12)^2 = s^2+s+\tfrac14 > s^2+s$ gives $\sqrt{s^2+s} < s + \tfrac12$, hence
$\delta < u$. Since $u$ enters only as an overall factor, $\delta/u$ depends on $A$
alone: the calibration is *scale free*.
</details>

For the measured amplitude $A = 0.1163$ this returns a relative spread
$\delta/u \approx 0.626$; the null control amplitude $0.0269$ would return
$\approx 0.372$.

---

## 5. The manhunt that had to fail

The natural response to an anomaly is to look for a *carrier*: a single binary feature
of each hit which, once conditioned on, makes the anomaly disappear. The pre-registered
bar was "removes at least 60% of the amplitude, leaves every stratum quiet". The
candidates were the obvious ones — $2 \mid v$, $3 \mid v$, $5 \mid v$, $7 \mid v$,
small-prime-factor-count terciles.

**Every single one removed 0%.**

That is not bad luck; it is a theorem. Because the primes act essentially independently,
the total log-amplitude is a sum of per-prime contributions

$$A = \sum_{i=1}^{k}\log E_{q_i}(c), \qquad E_q(c) = 1 + \Big(1-\tfrac1q\Big)X, \qquad X = \frac{(c-1)^2}{2c},$$

and the shape factor $X$ is **the same for every prime**. The only prime-dependence is
the factor $1 - 1/q$, which lies in $[2/3, 1)$ for every odd prime. Concavity of
$\log(1+\cdot)$ then squeezes all the contributions into a factor $3/2$ of each other,
giving the share bound

$$\frac{\log E_{q_j}(c)}{A} \;\le\; \frac{3}{2k}.$$

With $k \ge 3$ primes, the best any single covariate can do is $50\%$ — below the
$60\%$ bar. With $k \ge 5$, below $30\%$. Toggle the primes and drag the weight:

{{interactive_demo:1}}

<details>
<summary><b>The concavity squeeze, in full</b></summary>

For $Y \ge 0$ and $\theta \in [0,1]$, concavity of $\log$ applied to the points $1$ and
$1+Y$ with weights $1-\theta, \theta$ gives $\theta\log(1+Y) \le \log(1+\theta Y)$.
Apply this with $\theta = 2/3 \le 1 - 1/q$: every prime contributes at least
$\tfrac23 L$, where $L = \log(1+X)$, and clearly at most $L$. Hence
$A \ge k \cdot \tfrac23 L$ while any single $\log E_{q_j} \le L$, so the share is at
most $L / (\tfrac{2k}{3}L) = \tfrac{3}{2k}$.

The consequence for the experiment is a *structural* one: no amount of extra data can
make a per-hit binary covariate carry more than $3/(2k)$ of the hump. The covariate
family is removed from the search space, and the modelling target becomes the mixture
itself.
</details>

And here is the same result drawn against the two-point root-count distribution that
generates it:

{{visualization:1}}

---

## 6. From a negative result to a measuring instrument

Run the share bound backwards and the amplitude becomes a *prime counter*. If the
excess is spread nearly uniformly over $k$ primes, then

$$\frac{A}{X} \;\le\; k \;\le\; \frac{3}{2}\cdot\frac{A}{\log(1+X)}.$$

The bracket always contains the true $k$ and tightens toward a factor of $3/2$ as the
weight approaches $1$. The routine below performs both the calibration and the
tomography in closed form:

{{algorithm:1}}

---

## 7. Everything at once

The full demonstration below verifies each result numerically from scratch: mean
preservation at prime, prime-power and composite moduli; the exact over-dispersion
identity; the functional and generating identities against brute-force enumeration;
the Jensen gap for a family of convex functionals; the $3/(2k)$ share ceiling; the
closed-form hump and its exact inversion; and a direct sieve experiment on $j^2 - N$
showing individual moduli sitting at $2/q$ or $0$ while the population average lands
exactly on $1/q$.

{{demo:0}}

---

## 8. What to take away

1. **The naive baseline is unbiased on average and wrong for every individual $N$.**
   Mean preservation is exact at every modulus, so the error is invisible in the
   aggregate and unavoidable in any single sieve run.
2. **Convexity fixes the sign.** Because the smoothness functional is convex in the
   divisibility rates, over-dispersion always pushes the yield *up*. A hump is not
   merely consistent with the arithmetic; it is compelled by it.
3. **The excess is second-order.** It is quadratic in the deviation $c-1$: a variance
   effect distributed across the primes, not a first-order shift attached to any one of
   them.
4. **Hence no carrier — provably.** Any single per-hit binary covariate is capped at
   $3/(2k)$ of the amplitude. A uniform table of "0% removed" is the expected
   observation, not a failed search.
5. **And the amplitude is data.** Through
   $H = \tfrac12\log(1+\delta^2/(4u(u-\delta)))$ and its exact, scale-free inversion,
   a fitted hump measures the spread of the underlying divisibility mixture — and
   brackets how many primes produced it.

The practical upshot for anyone predicting sieve yield: replace the pointwise Dickman
value by a mixture over the residue classes of $N$ modulo the small primes. It costs
one Legendre symbol per prime, and it is the difference between a baseline that is
right on average and one that is right for the number you are actually factoring.

# U065 — Cycle 3: the mixture excess needs no primality, and tight two-sided bounds on
the per-prime share

Cycles 1–2 worked with odd primes, where the root-count distribution is the explicit
two-point mixture `{0, 2}` (plus the single fixed point `a = 0`).  This cycle isolates
what is really responsible for the effect.

* `sum_rootCountM` — for **every** modulus `m`, the number of solutions of `j² ≡ N`
  averages to exactly `1` over `N`: the divisibility rate of `v = j² − N` at `m` always
  has the naive `1/m` mean.  This is pure fibre counting; primality plays no role.
* `mixture_convex_excess_general` — consequently, for every convex functional `G`,
  `m · G 1 ≤ ∑_N G(#{j : m ∣ j² − N})`.  Mean preservation plus convexity is the entire
  mechanism; the arithmetic of quadratic residues only fixes the *size* of the effect.
* `exists_rootCountM_eq_zero` — for `m ≥ 3` the rate is genuinely non-constant: some
  target has no square roots at all, because `x ↦ x²` identifies `x` with `−x`.  So the
  mixture is never degenerate and the excess is never vacuous.
* `logExcess_sandwich` — a non-asymptotic two-sided bound
  `Y/(1+Y) ≤ log (excessRatio q c) ≤ Y` with `Y = (1 − 1/q)(c−1)²/(2c)`, pinning the
  per-prime hump share to the variance term up to a factor `1 + Y`.
-/
import Computation.U065NoSingleCarrier

namespace U065

open Finset

section GeneralModulus

variable {m : ℕ} [NeZero m]

/-- Root count for an arbitrary modulus: the number of residues `j` mod `m` with
`m ∣ j² − a`. -/
noncomputable def rootCountM {m : ℕ} [NeZero m] (a : ZMod m) : ℕ :=
  (Finset.univ.filter (fun x : ZMod m => x ^ 2 = a)).card

/-- For a prime modulus this is the root count of `U065QRMixture`. -/
theorem rootCountM_eq_rootCount {p : ℕ} [Fact p.Prime] (a : ZMod p) :
    rootCountM a = rootCount p a := rfl

/-- **Mean preservation for every modulus.**  Summing the number of solutions of
`j² ≡ N (mod m)` over all targets `N` gives exactly `m`. -/
theorem sum_rootCountM : ∑ a : ZMod m, rootCountM a = m := by
  classical
  have hcard : (Finset.univ : Finset (ZMod m)).card = m := ZMod.card m
  have h := Finset.card_eq_sum_card_fiberwise
    (f := fun x : ZMod m => x ^ 2) (s := (Finset.univ : Finset (ZMod m)))
    (t := (Finset.univ : Finset (ZMod m))) (fun x _ => Finset.mem_univ _)
  rw [hcard] at h
  simpa [rootCountM] using h.symm

/-- **The general mechanism.**  For any modulus and any convex functional of the
divisibility rate, the mixture average is at least the naive baseline value. -/
theorem mixture_convex_excess_general {G : ℝ → ℝ} (hG : ConvexOn ℝ Set.univ G) :
    (m : ℝ) * G 1 ≤ ∑ a : ZMod m, G ((rootCountM a : ℝ)) := by
  classical
  have hm0 : (0 : ℝ) < m := by
    have : 0 < m := Nat.pos_of_ne_zero (NeZero.ne m)
    exact_mod_cast this
  have hcard : (Finset.univ : Finset (ZMod m)).card = m := ZMod.card m
  have hw : ∀ a ∈ (Finset.univ : Finset (ZMod m)), (0 : ℝ) ≤ 1 / (m : ℝ) := by
    intro a _; positivity
  have hw1 : ∑ _a : ZMod m, (1 / (m : ℝ)) = 1 := by
    rw [Finset.sum_const, hcard, nsmul_eq_mul]
    field_simp
  have hmean : ∑ a : ZMod m, (1 / (m : ℝ)) • ((rootCountM a : ℝ)) = 1 := by
    have hsum : ∑ a : ZMod m, ((rootCountM a : ℝ)) = (m : ℝ) := by
      have := sum_rootCountM (m := m)
      exact_mod_cast congrArg (fun n : ℕ => (n : ℝ)) this
    simp only [smul_eq_mul, ← Finset.mul_sum, hsum]
    field_simp
  have hJ := hG.map_sum_le (t := (Finset.univ : Finset (ZMod m)))
    (w := fun _ => 1 / (m : ℝ)) (p := fun a => ((rootCountM a : ℝ))) hw hw1
    (fun a _ => Set.mem_univ _)
  rw [hmean] at hJ
  simp only [smul_eq_mul, ← Finset.mul_sum] at hJ
  calc (m : ℝ) * G 1 ≤ (m : ℝ) * ((1 / (m : ℝ)) * ∑ a : ZMod m, G ((rootCountM a : ℝ))) := by
        exact mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left hJ hm0.le
    _ = ∑ a : ZMod m, G ((rootCountM a : ℝ)) := by field_simp

/-- **The rate is never constant for `m ≥ 3`.**  Since `x ↦ x²` identifies `x` with
`−x`, the squaring map is not injective, hence not surjective, so some target has no
square roots: the mixture always has a genuine zero stratum. -/
theorem exists_rootCountM_eq_zero (hm : 3 ≤ m) : ∃ a : ZMod m, rootCountM a = 0 := by
  classical
  haveI : Fact (2 < m) := ⟨by omega⟩
  have hne : (1 : ZMod m) ≠ -1 := fun h => ZMod.neg_one_ne_one h.symm
  have hnotinj : ¬ Function.Injective (fun x : ZMod m => x ^ 2) := by
    intro hinj
    exact hne (hinj (by simp))
  have hnotsurj : ¬ Function.Surjective (fun x : ZMod m => x ^ 2) := fun hsurj =>
    hnotinj (Finite.injective_iff_surjective.mpr hsurj)

  (Finset.univ.filter (fun x : ZMod p => x ^ 2 = a)).card

  rw [ZMod.ringChar_zmod_n]; exact hp

  have h := (Fact.out (p := p.Prime)).two_le
  have h3 : 3 ≤ p := by omega
  exact_mod_cast h3

  have := quadraticChar_card_sqrts (F := ZMod p) (ringChar_ne_two hp) a
  rw [← this]

from __future__ import annotations

import math
import random
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Root counts and mean preservation
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def root_counts(m: int) -> List[int]:
    """X_m(a) = #{x mod m : x^2 = a} for every target a in Z/m."""
    counts = [0] * m
    for x in range(m):
        counts[(x * x) % m] += 1
    return counts


def mean_preservation_check(m: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Return (sum of root counts, m).  The theorem says they are equal."""
    return sum(root_counts(m)), m


def over_dispersion(p: int) -> int:
    """sum_a (X_p(a) - 1)^2 ; equals p - 1 for every odd prime p."""
    return sum((c - 1) ** 2 for c in root_counts(p))


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Exact functional / generating identities
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def functional_sum_bruteforce(p: int, g: Callable[[int], float]) -> float:
    """sum_a g(X_p(a)) by direct enumeration."""
    return sum(g(c) for c in root_counts(p))


def functional_sum_formula(p: int, g: Callable[[int], float]) -> float:
    """g(1) + (p-1)(g(2)+g(0))/2 -- the exact functional identity."""
    return g(1) + (p - 1) * (g(2) + g(0)) / 2.0


def generating_sum_formula(p: int, c: float) -> float:
    """p c + (p-1)(c-1)^2/2 -- naive baseline plus mixture excess."""
    return p * c + (p - 1) * (c - 1) ** 2 / 2.0


def excess_ratio(q: int, c: float) -> float:
    """E_q(c) = 1 + (1 - 1/q) (c-1)^2 / (2c)."""
    return 1.0 + (1.0 - 1.0 / q) * shape_factor(c)


def shape_factor(c: float) -> float:
    """X = (c-1)^2 / (2c), the prime-independent shape of the excess."""
    return (c - 1.0) ** 2 / (2.0 * c)


def log_excess(q: int, c: float) -> float:
    """Per-prime contribution to the hump log-amplitude."""
    return math.log(excess_ratio(q, c))


def hump_log_amplitude(primes: Sequence[int], c: float) -> float:
    """A = sum_q log E_q(c)."""
    return sum(log_excess(q, c) for q in primes)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Convexity mechanism
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def jensen_gap(m: int, G: Callable[[float], float]) -> float:
    """sum_a G(X_m(a)) - m G(1) ; nonnegative for convex G, positive for m>=3
    and strictly convex G."""
    return sum(G(float(c)) for c in root_counts(m)) - m * G(1.0)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Dickman branch, hump, calibration
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def rho1(u: float) -> float:
    """First Dickman branch rho(u) = 1 - log u, valid on [1, 2]."""
    return 1.0 - math.log(u)


def hump_amp_definition(u: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """(rho(u) + rho(u-d))/2 - rho(u - d/2), computed from the definition."""
    return (rho1(u) + rho1(u - delta)) / 2.0 - rho1(u - delta / 2.0)


def hump_amp_closed_form(u: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """(1/2) log(1 + d^2 / (4 u (u - d)))."""
    return 0.5 * math.log(1.0 + delta ** 2 / (4.0 * u * (u - delta)))


def calibrated_spread(u: float, A: float) -> float:
    """Exact inverse: the spread reproducing a measured amplitude A."""
    s = math.exp(2.0 * A) - 1.0
    return 2.0 * u * (math.sqrt(s * s + s) - s)


def carrier_count_bracket(A: float, c: float) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """A/X <= k <= (3/2) A / log(1+X) with X = (c-1)^2/(2c)."""
    X = shape_factor(c)
    return A / X, 1.5 * A / math.log(1.0 + X)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. A direct sieve experiment
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def sieve_divisibility_rate(N: int, q: int, window: int) -> float:
    """Observed density of q | (j^2 - N) for j in a window above sqrt(N)."""
    j0 = math.isqrt(N) + 1
    hits = sum(1 for j in range(j0, j0 + window) if (j * j - N) % q == 0)
    return hits / window


def legendre_root_count(N: int, q: int) -> int:
    """Predicted X_q(N) = number of solutions of j^2 = N mod q."""
    return sum(1 for x in range(q) if (x * x - N) % q == 0)

-- NEW_FILE: Catalog/MachineLearning/EdgeSpikeCensoring.lean
import Mathlib

/-!
# Edge-spike censoring: why the steepness of a left-edge spike is a lower bound only

## Motivation (exp 594 / paper 245, round-88 identifiability audit)

A pooled positional histogram was fitted with a two-component profile,
*flat bulk + left-edge spike*, where the spike is an exponential law with rate
`b` truncated to the unit interval.  Empirically the fitted `b_edge` "rode the
cap": it landed at `40.000` when the optimiser was capped at `40` and at `40.46`
when capped at `80`, with a bootstrap CI `[15.25, 80.0]` whose upper end is the
cap itself.  The registered analysis therefore had to be amended to
*"left-edge spike with `b_edge ≳ 15`, **lower bound only**"*.

This file proves that this behaviour is **not** an artefact of the optimiser:
it is a theorem about the model class.  Once the observable is the *mass in the
edge bin* `[0, t]`, the map `b ↦` (edge mass) is strictly increasing but
bounded, and it approaches its ceiling at rate `exp (-b t)`.  Consequently:

* `EdgeSpike.binLogLik_cap_riding` — the binned log-likelihood is **strictly
  increasing in `b`** whenever the empirical edge fraction is at least the
  ceiling `edgeProbLimit`.  Hence for every cap `B` the constrained optimum sits
  exactly at `b = B`: cap-riding is forced.
* `EdgeSpike.no_finite_maximiser` — no finite maximiser exists, so no cap raise
  produces an interior optimum.
* `EdgeSpike.cap_gain_le` — the total remaining log-likelihood available above a
  cap `B` is at most `C · exp (-B t)`.  Raising the cap buys exponentially
  little: at the audited geometry this is why `dAICc` moved only from `-101.28`
  to `-101.33` between caps `40` and `80`.

The three statements together are the formal content of the verdict
`H0_SPIKE_STEEPNESS_UNIDENTIFIABLE`: the data censor the steepness parameter.
-/

namespace EdgeSpike

open Real Filter Topology

/-- CDF at `t` of the exponential law with rate `b` truncated to `[0,1]`;
this is the mass that a left-edge spike of steepness `b` puts in the edge bin
`[0, t]`. -/
noncomputable def truncExpCDF (b t : ℝ) : ℝ := (1 - exp (-(b * t))) / (1 - exp (-b))

/-- Edge-bin probability of the *flat bulk + left-edge spike* profile:
a fraction `1 - rho` of the mass is uniform on `[0,1]` and a fraction `rho`
follows the truncated exponential of steepness `b`. -/
noncomputable def edgeProb (rho t b : ℝ) : ℝ := (1 - rho) * t + rho * truncExpCDF b t

/-- The `b → ∞` ceiling of `edgeProb`: the spike degenerates to a point mass at
the left edge, i.e. the whole spike component lands in the edge bin. -/
noncomputable def edgeProbLimit (rho t : ℝ) : ℝ := (1 - rho) * t + rho

/-- Per-observation binned log-likelihood of the two-cell (edge vs. bulk) table
with empirical edge fraction `h` and model edge probability `p`. -/
noncomputable def binLogLik (h p : ℝ) : ℝ := h * log p + (1 - h) * log (1 - p)

section Basic

variable {b t : ℝ}

lemma one_sub_exp_neg_pos (hb : 0 < b) : 0 < 1 - exp (-b) := by
  have : exp (-b) < 1 := Real.exp_lt_one_iff.mpr (by linarith)
  linarith

lemma truncExpCDF_pos (hb : 0 < b) (ht : 0 < t) : 0 < truncExpCDF b t := by
  have hden := one_sub_exp_neg_pos hb
  have hnum : 0 < 1 - exp (-(b * t)) := by
    have : exp (-(b * t)) < 1 := Real.exp_lt_one_iff.mpr (by nlinarith)
    linarith
  exact div_pos hnum hden

lemma truncExpCDF_lt_one (hb : 0 < b) (ht1 : t < 1) :
    truncExpCDF b t < 1 := by
  have hden := one_sub_exp_neg_pos hb
  have hlt : exp (-b) < exp (-(b * t)) := by
    apply Real.exp_lt_exp.mpr; nlinarith
  unfold truncExpCDF
  rw [div_lt_one hden]
  linarith

lemma truncExpCDF_le_one (hb : 0 < b) (ht1 : t ≤ 1) : truncExpCDF b t ≤ 1 := by
  have hden := one_sub_exp_neg_pos hb
  have hlt : exp (-b) ≤ exp (-(b * t)) := by
    apply Real.exp_le_exp.mpr; nlinarith
  unfold truncExpCDF
  rw [div_le_one hden]
  linarith

end Basic

section Convexity

/-- Strict convexity of `exp` on `[0, b]`: the chord inequality that drives the

  to `-101.33` between caps `40` and `80`.

  have hcmp : (1 - h) * ((q - p) / (1 - q)) ≤ h * ((q - p) / q) := by
    rw [show (1 - h) * ((q - p) / (1 - q)) = ((1 - h) * (q - p)) / (1 - q) by ring,
      show h * ((q - p) / q) = (h * (q - p)) / q by ring,
      div_le_div_iff₀ (show (0 : ℝ) < 1 - q by linarith) hq0]
    nlinarith [mul_nonneg (sub_pos.mpr hpq).le (sub_nonneg.mpr hqh)]
  have hA : h * ((q - p) / q) < h * (log q - log p) := mul_lt_mul_of_pos_left hL hh0
  have hB : (1 - h) * (-((q - p) / (1 - q))) < (1 - h) * (log (1 - q) - log (1 - p)) :=
    mul_lt_mul_of_pos_left hM (by linarith)
  unfold binLogLik
  nlinarith [hA, hB, hcmp]

lemma edgeProb_lt_limit (hrho : 0 < rho) (hb : 0 < b) (ht1 : t < 1) :
    edgeProb rho t b < edgeProbLimit rho t := by
  unfold edgeProb edgeProbLimit
  have := truncExpCDF_lt_one hb ht1
  nlinarith

lemma edgeProb_pos (hrho0 : 0 < rho) (hrho1 : rho < 1) (hb : 0 < b) (ht0 : 0 < t) :
    0 < edgeProb rho t b := by
  unfold edgeProb
  have := truncExpCDF_pos hb ht0
  nlinarith

lemma edgeProb_strictMonoOn (hrho : 0 < rho) (ht0 : 0 < t) (ht1 : t < 1) :
    StrictMonoOn (fun b => edgeProb rho t b) (Set.Ioi 0) := by
  intro x hx y hy hxy
  have hmono : truncExpCDF x t < truncExpCDF y t :=
    truncExpCDF_strictMonoOn ht0 ht1 hx hy hxy
  show edgeProb rho t x < edgeProb rho t y
  unfold edgeProb
  nlinarith

/-- **Cap-riding is forced.**  If the empirical edge fraction is at least the
`b → ∞` ceiling of the model, then the binned log-likelihood is strictly
increasing in the steepness `b`; hence, for any cap `B`, the constrained
maximiser is the cap itself. -/
theorem binLogLik_cap_riding (hrho0 : 0 < rho) (hrho1 : rho < 1) (ht0 : 0 < t)
    (ht1 : t < 1) (hh : edgeProbLimit rho t ≤ h) (hh1 : h < 1) {b B : ℝ}
    (hb : 0 < b) (hbB : b < B) :
    binLogLik h (edgeProb rho t b) < binLogLik h (edgeProb rho t B) := by
  have hB : 0 < B := lt_trans hb hbB
  have hmono : edgeProb rho t b < edgeProb rho t B :=
    edgeProb_strictMonoOn hrho0 ht0 ht1 (Set.mem_Ioi.mpr hb) (Set.mem_Ioi.mpr hB) hbB
  have hpos := edgeProb_pos hrho0 hrho1 hb ht0
  have hBlt : edgeProb rho t B < edgeProbLimit rho t := edgeProb_lt_limit hrho0 hB ht1
  have hLpos : 0 < edgeProbLimit rho t := by
    unfold edgeProbLimit; nlinarith
  exact binLogLik_lt (lt_of_lt_of_le hLpos hh) hh1 hpos hmono
    (le_trans hBlt.le hh)

/-- **No finite maximiser.**  Every steepness value is beaten by a larger one:
the MLE does not exist in `(0, ∞)`, so no cap raise can produce an interior
optimum — only a new boundary solution. -/
theorem no_finite_maximiser (hrho0 : 0 < rho) (hrho1 : rho < 1) (ht0 : 0 < t)
    (ht1 : t < 1) (hh : edgeProbLimit rho t ≤ h) (hh1 : h < 1) (hb : 0 < b) :
    ∃ b' > b, binLogLik h (edgeProb rho t b) < binLogLik h (edgeProb rho t b') :=
  ⟨b + 1, by linarith,
    binLogLik_cap_riding hrho0 hrho1 ht0 ht1 hh hh1 hb (by linarith)⟩

/-- **Exponentially small cap gains.**  All the log-likelihood that remains
above a cap `b` is bounded by `C · exp (-b t)` with
`C = 2 rho / min ((1-rho) t) (1 - edgeProbLimit rho t)`.  Raising the cap
therefore buys exponentially little, whatever the data. -/
theorem cap_gain_le (hrho0 : 0 < rho) (hrho1 : rho < 1) (ht0 : 0 < t) (ht1 : t < 1)
    (hh0 : 0 ≤ h) (hh1 : h ≤ 1) (hb : 1 ≤ b) :
    binLogLik h (edgeProbLimit rho t) - binLogLik h (edgeProb rho t b) ≤
      (2 * rho / min ((1 - rho) * t) (1 - edgeProbLimit rho t)) * exp (-(b * t)) := by
  have hb0 : (0 : ℝ) < b := lt_of_lt_of_le zero_lt_one hb
  set p := edgeProb rho t b with hpdef
  set P := edgeProbLimit rho t with hPdef
  have hPlt : P < 1 := by rw [hPdef]; unfold edgeProbLimit; nlinarith
  have hlow : (1 - rho) * t ≤ p := by
    rw [hpdef]; unfold edgeProb
    have := truncExpCDF_pos hb0 ht0
    nlinarith
  have hlowpos : 0 < (1 - rho) * t := by nlinarith
  have hppos : 0 < p := lt_of_lt_of_le hlowpos hlow
  have hpP : p < P := edgeProb_lt_limit hrho0 hb0 ht1
  have hdiff : P - p ≤ 2 * rho * exp (-(b * t)) := by
    rw [hpdef, hPdef]; unfold edgeProb edgeProbLimit
    have hcen := one_sub_truncExpCDF_le hb ht1.le
    nlinarith
  have hdiffnn : 0 ≤ P - p := by linarith
  set m := min ((1 - rho) * t) (1 - P) with hmdef
  have hmpos : 0 < m := lt_min hlowpos (by linarith)
  have hm1 : m ≤ p := le_trans (min_le_left _ _) hlow
  have hm2 : m ≤ 1 - P := min_le_right _ _
  have hlog1 : log P - log p ≤ (P - p) / m := by
    have hx : 0 < P / p := div_pos (lt_trans hppos hpP) hppos
    have hlog := Real.log_le_sub_one_of_pos hx
    rw [Real.log_div (ne_of_gt (lt_trans hppos hpP)) (ne_of_gt hppos)] at hlog
    have h2 : P / p - 1 = (P - p) / p := by field_simp
    rw [h2] at hlog
    exact le_trans hlog (div_le_div_of_nonneg_left hdiffnn hmpos hm1)
  have hlog2 : log (1 - P) - log (1 - p) ≤ (P - p) / m := by
    have hmono : log (1 - P) ≤ log (1 - p) :=
      Real.log_le_log (by linarith) (by linarith)
    have hnn : 0 ≤ (P - p) / m := div_nonneg hdiffnn hmpos.le
    linarith
  have hbound : (P - p) / m ≤ (2 * rho / m) * exp (-(b * t)) := by
    rw [show (2 * rho / m) * exp (-(b * t)) = (2 * rho * exp (-(b * t))) / m by ring,
      div_le_div_iff₀ hmpos hmpos]
    nlinarith [mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_right hdiff hmpos.le]
  have hsum : binLogLik h P - binLogLik h p ≤ (P - p) / m := by
    unfold binLogLik
    have hA : h * (log P - log p) ≤ h * ((P - p) / m) :=
      mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left hlog1 hh0
    have hB : (1 - h) * (log (1 - P) - log (1 - p)) ≤ (1 - h) * ((P - p) / m) :=
      mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left hlog2 (by linarith)
    nlinarith [hA, hB]
  linarith [hsum, hbound]

end Likelihood

section IdentifiedSet

variable {rho t : ℝ}

/-- **The identified set contains a ray.**  If the observed edge mass `v` sits
within the tolerance `eps` of the ceiling, then *every* steepness above a
threshold `B₀` (any `B₀ ≥ 1` with `2 rho exp (-B₀ t) ≤ eps`) is compatible with
the data: there is no finite upper confidence limit for `b`. -/
theorem identified_ray (hrho0 : 0 < rho) (hrho1 : rho < 1) (ht0 : 0 < t) (ht1 : t < 1)
    {v eps B₀ b : ℝ} (hv1 : edgeProbLimit rho t - eps ≤ v)
    (hv2 : v ≤ edgeProbLimit rho t) (hB0 : 1 ≤ B₀)
    (hB0' : 2 * rho * exp (-(B₀ * t)) ≤ eps) (hb : B₀ ≤ b) :
    |edgeProb rho t b - v| ≤ eps := by
  have hb1 : (1 : ℝ) ≤ b := le_trans hB0 hb
  have hb0 : (0 : ℝ) < b := lt_of_lt_of_le zero_lt_one hb1
  have hple : edgeProb rho t b < edgeProbLimit rho t := edgeProb_lt_limit hrho0 hb0 ht1
  have hcen := one_sub_truncExpCDF_le hb1 ht1.le
  have hgap : edgeProbLimit rho t - edgeProb rho t b ≤ 2 * rho * exp (-(b * t)) := by
    unfold edgeProb edgeProbLimit
    nlinarith
  have hmono : exp (-(b * t)) ≤ exp (-(B₀ * t)) :=
    Real.exp_le_exp.mpr (by nlinarith)
  have hsmall : edgeProbLimit rho t - edgeProb rho t b ≤ eps := by
    have : 2 * rho * exp (-(b * t)) ≤ 2 * rho * exp (-(B₀ * t)) := by nlinarith
    linarith
  rw [abs_le]
  constructor <;> linarith

/-- Such a threshold always exists: the identified set is genuinely unbounded
above. -/
theorem exists_ray_threshold (ht0 : 0 < t) {eps : ℝ} (heps : 0 < eps) :
    ∃ B₀ : ℝ, 1 ≤ B₀ ∧ 2 * rho * exp (-(B₀ * t)) ≤ eps := by
  have hlim : Tendsto (fun b : ℝ => 2 * rho * exp (-(b * t))) atTop (𝓝 0) := by
    have h1 : Tendsto (fun b : ℝ => -(b * t)) atTop atBot := by
      have h2 : Tendsto (fun b : ℝ => b * t) atTop atTop :=
        Filter.Tendsto.atTop_mul_const ht0 tendsto_id
      exact tendsto_neg_atTop_atBot.comp h2
    simpa using (Real.tendsto_exp_atBot.comp h1).const_mul (2 * rho)
  have hev : ∀ᶠ b : ℝ in atTop, 2 * rho * exp (-(b * t)) < eps :=
    hlim.eventually (Iio_mem_nhds heps)
  obtain ⟨B, hB⟩ := (hev.and (eventually_ge_atTop (1 : ℝ))).exists
  exact ⟨B, hB.2, hB.1.le⟩

/-- **Lower bounds do survive.**  Any steepness whose edge mass falls short of
the observed value by more than the tolerance is excluded, and by strict
monotonicity so is every smaller steepness.  Together with `identified_ray`
this is the amended verdict: the identified set for `b` is of the form
"`b ≳ b₁`", with no upper limit. -/
theorem below_threshold_excluded (hrho0 : 0 < rho) (ht0 : 0 < t) (ht1 : t < 1)
    {v eps b b₁ : ℝ} (heps : 0 ≤ eps) (hb : 0 < b) (hbb : b ≤ b₁)
    (hexcl : edgeProb rho t b₁ + eps < v) :
    eps < |edgeProb rho t b - v| := by
  have hb1 : 0 < b₁ := lt_of_lt_of_le hb hbb
  have hmono : edgeProb rho t b ≤ edgeProb rho t b₁ := by
    rcases eq_or_lt_of_le hbb with h | h
    · rw [h]
    · exact (edgeProb_strictMonoOn hrho0 ht0 ht1 (Set.mem_Ioi.mpr hb)
        (Set.mem_Ioi.mpr hb1) h).le
  have hlt : edgeProb rho t b + eps < v := by linarith
  have : eps < v - edgeProb rho t b := by linarith
  calc eps < v - edgeProb rho t b := this
    _ = |edgeProb rho t b - v| := by
        rw [abs_sub_comm, abs_of_pos (by linarith)]

/-- **Population identification does hold.**  Whenever the observed edge mass is
bracketed by two model values, exactly one steepness reproduces it.  So the
non-identifiability audited here is a *tolerance* phenomenon (the ray of
`identified_ray`), not a failure of the population map: the model is injective
in `b`, but its image is exponentially compressed near the ceiling. -/
theorem unique_steepness_of_bracket (hrho0 : 0 < rho) (ht0 : 0 < t) (ht1 : t < 1)
    {v b₀ b₁ : ℝ} (hb0 : 0 < b₀) (hb01 : b₀ ≤ b₁)
    (h1 : edgeProb rho t b₀ ≤ v) (h2 : v ≤ edgeProb rho t b₁) :
    ∃! b : ℝ, b ∈ Set.Icc b₀ b₁ ∧ edgeProb rho t b = v := by
  have hcont : ContinuousOn (fun b => edgeProb rho t b) (Set.Icc b₀ b₁) := by
    intro x hx
    have hx0 : 0 < x := lt_of_lt_of_le hb0 hx.1
    have hca : ContinuousAt (fun b => edgeProb rho t b) x := by
      have h := (hasDerivAt_truncExpCDF x t hx0).continuousAt
      unfold edgeProb
      exact continuousAt_const.add (continuousAt_const.mul h)
    exact hca.continuousWithinAt
  obtain ⟨b, hbmem, hbv⟩ := intermediate_value_Icc hb01 hcont ⟨h1, h2⟩
  refine ⟨b, ⟨hbmem, hbv⟩, ?_⟩
  rintro b' ⟨hb'mem, hb'v⟩
  have hinj := (edgeProb_strictMonoOn hrho0 ht0 ht1).injOn
  exact hinj (Set.mem_Ioi.mpr (lt_of_lt_of_le hb0 hb'mem.1))
    (Set.mem_Ioi.mpr (lt_of_lt_of_le hb0 hbmem.1)) (by simpa using hb'v.trans hbv.symm)

end IdentifiedSet

end EdgeSpike
